1.pericope_label: In the last days perilous times shall come; lovers of their own selves

schools.summary: Settle what the last days are before anything else, and say that the common answer is probably wrong. Most refer the phrase to the period immediately preceding the second coming; but the epistle that calls its own moment the last time points instead to a long stretch running from the first advent to the second. Support it from the rabbinic division of history into this age and the age to come, and from the talmudic scheme of six thousand years. Then handle the catalogue that follows. Report the attempt to sort the vices into three groups of five, six and seven, and reject it as artificial, since preserving the groups forces a strained sense on some terms. Note that most of the list recurs in the opening chapter of Romans, and that the first term appears nowhere else in the New Testament. Draw the necessary distinction on self-love: a regard for oneself that secures one's own salvation is proper and injures nobody; what is condemned tramples the rights and comforts of others.

Refuse to let the times take the blame. The writer censures not the days nor the seasons but the men of them, for it is our habit to call an age good or evil from what men do in it. Then show why the warning is repeated at all, and how: it is given three ways, from prophecy, from the past example of those who withstood Moses, and from plain reasoning about the vessels in a great house. The purpose of all three is to keep the hearer from being troubled, since if such men existed in Moses's day and will exist afterwards, it is no wonder they exist now. Finally name the root from which the rest of the list grows, which is overweeningness: the man seized by it grows careless even of his own interests, for we are members one of another, and the injury of a neighbour is not confined to him but distracts the whole body.

Take the prediction as a spur rather than a threat. When matters go to our wish we grow careless, but necessity urges us keenly; so the church is told it will be subject to terrible diseases requiring uncommon fidelity, diligence, watchfulness and unwearied constancy in its pastors. So far from giving way or being terrified by difficulties, we ought to rouse our hearts for resistance. Say plainly what the phrase covers: the universal condition of the Christian church, not one age compared with another. And name the fancy it corrects, which was common then and is common still -- that because the prophets promised everything would be astonishingly reformed under Messiah's kingdom, we must now be in a state of angelical holiness, with no more vices in the world. There will not be, even under the gospel.

Refuse to aim the passage at anyone's favourite enemy, and say why. Catholics apply this description to Protestants and Protestants to Catholics; one scholar applies it to the Jews and others to heretics generally; but there have been teachers and people in every age of the church and of the world to whom the words legitimately apply, and both parties have been lovers of their own selves. Allow the phrase about the last days its breadth -- it often means the days of Messiah, is sometimes stretched to the destruction of Jerusalem as the last days of the Jewish state, and may mean any future near or distant. Then work the catalogue by its etymologies, which repay it: the proud are airy and trifling persons who are all outside, the unthankful are those without grace or gracefulness, and mark that the vices are found even in the church, in great numbers and to a higher degree than ever.

Begin by removing the offence, since a hearer who finds bad men in the church will be tempted to think the worse of religion for it. The net of the gospel was to enclose both good fish and bad; even in gold ore there is dross, and much chaff among the wheat on the floor; and seducers were foretold, so we must not be offended when they come. Then locate the real danger, which is not what most expect. Gospel times were times of reformation, yet perilous times come in them -- not so much from persecution without as from corruption within, so that it becomes difficult for a man to keep a good conscience. The mischief is done by such as have the form of godliness, and two traitors within a garrison may do it more hurt than an army before its walls.

debates.question: What period do "the last days" cover?

sides.position: Not the time immediately before the second coming, as most commentators hold, but a long period running from the first advent to the second, as the epistle that calls its own moment the last time implies
The gospel dispensation, commencing at the time of our Lord's death, is peculiarly so styled
The universal condition of the Christian church; the writer is not comparing his age with a later one but describing the future state of Christ's kingdom
Often the days of Messiah, sometimes extended to the destruction of Jerusalem as the last days of the Jewish state; but the phrase may mean any future time, near or distant
Gospel times, in which perilous times would come notwithstanding the reformation they brought

debates.question: Why are the times called perilous, and whose fault is it?

sides.position: Not the days nor the times are blamed but the men of them, as we call an age good or evil from what men do in it; the root of the whole list is overweeningness
Not chiefly persecution from without but corruption within, so that it becomes difficult to keep a good conscience; two traitors within a garrison do more hurt than an army before it
The church will be subject to terrible diseases requiring uncommon fidelity and constancy in its pastors; the prediction is meant to sharpen diligence, not to terrify
Delivered by a spirit of prophecy so that they might be prepared for such events and fortified against them

outliers.note: Alone refuses to let the times take the blame, observing that the writer censures not the days nor the seasons but the men of them, since we call an age good or evil from what men do in it; and alone traces the whole catalogue to a single root, the overweeningness that makes a man careless even of his own interests, since we are members one of another and a neighbour's injury is not confined to him.

Alone names the expectation the prediction corrects: that because the prophets promised everything would be astonishingly reformed under Messiah's kingdom, men imagined a condition absolutely peaceful and free from annoyance, and concluded that since the Redeemer's coming nothing but correct virtue would be seen and there would be no more vices in the world.

Alone declines to aim the passage at any party, observing that Catholics apply the description to Protestants and Protestants to Catholics, one scholar to the Jews and others to heretics generally, and that both parties have been lovers of their own selves.

Alone answers the offence a hearer feels at finding bad men in the church, with the net that enclosed good fish and bad, the dross in gold ore and the chaff among the wheat, and alone locates the danger inside rather than outside, two traitors within a garrison doing more hurt than an army before it.

themes: This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come
For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy

3.pericope_label: Without natural affection; having a form of godliness but denying the power

schools.summary: Most of this list is compound adjectives, so work it by the parts and keep moving. The word for truce-breakers comes from the drink-offering, libations of blood and wine having been poured at the making of treaties, so it means those bound by no promise; it may be taken either of the implacable who refuse reconciliation or of those who simply disregard agreements, and a society in which no compact holds is at its lowest point. The term for false accusers is the ordinary word for devils. Heady comes from falling forward, high-minded from smoke. Several of these words occur nowhere else in the New Testament. Then draw the distinction that gives the paragraph its force: the similar catalogue in Romans paints the sins of paganism, while this one describes a new paganism going under the name of Christianity -- which is why the response is graded, the pagan to be courteously entreated and these to be openly shunned.

Read the vices as a portrait of a particular corruption rather than of human nature at large, and be concrete about it: children put into cloisters against their will, priests obliged to quit their wives and declare their children spurious, princes assassinated, and secrets betrayed that were obtained under the seal of confession. Then take the form of godliness in its several possible senses -- a mere external show, with great pretended piety; or a plan of doctrine and scheme of truths which men may hold without partaking of the grace of God; or the scriptures themselves, professed and preserved by those who deny their power. The point in each case is the same, that the mask may be perfectly maintained while the thing itself is absent.

Give the etymologies, which carry the sense better than the English does. Without natural affection means lacking what parents bear their young and the young their parents, an affection common to every class of animals, so that men without it are worse than brutes; incontinent means those who have sinned away the power of self-government; fierce means whatever is contrary to pliability and gentleness. One word deserves a remark of its own: the term for despisers of the good does in one Greek word what English needs five or six for, and those who do not love the good must themselves be radically bad. On the form of godliness, take the noun as a sketch or summary, and apply it to those who keep all their religion in a creed, a confession, a catechism or a body of divinity while destitute of the life of God -- and who go on to deny that such life is to be experienced at all. Then press the command: not merely do not imitate them, but have no fellowship with them, for they are dangerous and seldom suspected, their outside being fair.

debates.question: Whom does the catalogue of vices indict?

sides.position: Nobody in particular, and the attempt to aim it is self-serving: Catholics apply it to Protestants and Protestants to Catholics, one scholar to the Jews and others to heretics, and both parties have been lovers of their own selves

A new paganism going under the name of Christianity: the similar catalogue in Romans paints the sins of paganism, this one the characteristics of those who wore the uniform of Christ and dishonoured his name
A great apostasy within the church, in which all these things have been practised and tolerated while no body of men has been more zealous in keeping up the forms of religion
The same, and in particulars: children put into cloisters against their will, priests made to quit their wives, secrets betrayed that were learnt in confession

outliers.note: Alone draws the distinction that gives the catalogue its point, that the similar list in Romans paints the sins of paganism while this one describes a new paganism going under the name of Christianity; and alone grades the response accordingly, the pagan to be courteously entreated but these to be openly shunned. He also alone notices the shape of the list, that it opens with the love of self, which excludes all love of others, and closes with the love of pleasure, which shuts out all love of God.

Alone pauses over the language rather than the vice, remarking that one Greek word does the work of five or six English ones and that those who do not love the good must themselves be radically bad; and alone reaches for a national example of treachery, those who delivered up their own king to his enemies, calling it a stain no lapse of ages can wipe out.

Alone fills the vices in with particulars from one quarter -- children put into cloisters against their will, priests obliged to quit their wives and declare their children spurious, and secrets betrayed that were obtained under the seal of confession.

themes: Without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good
Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof: from such turn away

6.pericope_label: Creeping into houses; as Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses

schools.summary: Be honest that the verb for creeping in is milder than the English suggests -- it means to enter or slip in, and the idea of cunning comes from the context rather than the word. Then supply the circumstance that gives the phrase its force: women in those countries lived in a seclusion that made real fraud necessary before their apartments could be reached. Note that the term for silly women is a contemptuous diminutive found only here. On the two magicians, say plainly that the names are not in the Old Testament, and then defend the tradition: nothing is likelier than that the names of the chief magicians who tried to match the miracles would be preserved, and they are found in the Targum, in Jewish sources and in several pagan and early Christian writers. Close on the promise that they shall proceed no further, and observe how it has held -- one school of error after another passing into disrepute, then neglect, then oblivion, while the church remains.

Note the figure the Syriac reached for in the verb of creeping, a word connected with the weasel, whose way in is sometimes covered and sometimes open. Then divide the blame for the perpetual learning that never arrives, and divide it evenly: partly the teachers heaped up, who are unapt to teach and are blind guides and enemies of the truth, and partly the hearers themselves, whose own lusts hinder them from coming to it. On the limit set to the deceivers, measure it by the precedent the text supplies: the magicians of Egypt did lying wonders and hardened Pharaoh and deceived a nation, but they could not destroy Israel nor hinder their departure when the time came; and so these can deceive but cannot prevail against the church, nor hinder the Lord's people from coming out.

Take the passage as a warning to congregations and not only about them. False teachers work through those who see in them a semblance of piety and entertain them eagerly; such cases are on record among the Jews and among the monks, but in what sect or party have such teachers not occasionally been found? No communion makes provision for such men. Then turn the verse about perpetual learning on the ordinary hearer, since it fits him: there are many who hear good sermons repeatedly and derive little profit, having no more grace now than several years ago, not because they have wickedly departed but because they do not meditate, do not think, and do not reduce what they hear to practice -- and under the preaching of an apostle they would still not become wise to salvation. On the two magicians, note that the word for seducers means jugglers and pretenders to magical arts, and that the church has in every age been disgraced by persons dealing in false miracles.

debates.question: Does the verb rendered "creep into" itself imply cunning?

sides.position: Not certainly; four renderings have been offered, and the idea of deceit comes from the complexion of the passage rather than from the word
It means to enter, to slip in by insinuation, and the same picture of stealthy creepers appears elsewhere
The Syriac chose a word connected with the weasel, whose way in is sometimes covered and sometimes open
Special fraud was needed, since women in Eastern lands lived in comparative seclusion and their apartments were hard to reach

debates.question: Why do these learners never arrive at the truth?

sides.position: A morbid love of novelty and a hope of penetrating mysteries not revealed to true teachers spurred them on, but their evil life hardened the heart
Partly the teachers heaped up, who are blind guides, and partly themselves, whose own lusts hinder them
Because the teaching itself never leads to truth; and the same is true of many who hear good sermons and do not meditate, think, or reduce what they hear to practice
They lack the intellectual power to cut through the fog of words, and yet pride themselves on belonging to the intelligentsia
Many learn the doctrines speculatively, or the government of the church, and remain strangers to the saving power of the gospel

outliers.note: Alone explains why women were the object, observing that the tempter began with Eve rather than Adam and that the advocates of error have followed the precedent, working through the weaker in order to reach the men; and alone lists four scholars' renderings of the verb before concluding that the idea of cunning is not certainly in the word itself.

Alone refuses to leave the problem in antiquity, naming two religious impostors of his own country and century who gathered women about them under the guise of religion, and alone reports the suggestion that the contemptuous diminutive means something like society ladies.

Alone specifies the method by which the false teachers won their following, that they supplied anodynes for consciences already burdened with sins, and alone reads the promise that they shall proceed no further as comfort deliberately offered after an unsparing diagnosis, noting that one school of error after another has passed into disrepute, then neglect, then oblivion, while the church remains.

themes: For of this sort are they which creep into houses, and lead captive silly women laden with sins
Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth
Now as Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses, so do these also resist the truth

10.pericope_label: Thou hast fully known my doctrine; all that will live godly shall suffer persecution

schools.summary: Correct the rendering first: the verb means to follow alongside and trace out step by step, not merely to have been told, and the same word describes an evangelist who traced events back to their source. Count the nouns it governs -- nine of them, seven belonging to this verse and two to the next. Then answer the question the passage raises: why these three cities out of a long history? For a general reader they were fair samples of what happened often afterwards, but for this reader they were the cities of the first missionary journey, some of the incidents among his earliest memories of the work and others just before he was taken as a companion. On the general rule that follows, gloss the participle as those who determine to live godly, note that the verb means to be hunted like wild beasts, and define persecution carefully: it consists in subjecting a man to injury or disadvantage for his opinions, which is a different thing from meeting those opinions with argument.

Explain why the doctrine is called his own, since the phrase can mislead: not as invented or contrived by him, but as received from God and preached purely, without adulteration or mixture, and openly, nothing profitable being kept back. Then take the three cities as evidence rather than as narrative -- they are named because they lie in the country where the hearer lived, so that he knew the truth of them not only from the writer's mouth but from the testimony of others, and may have witnessed some himself. On living godly, be exact about what is claimed: those who live according to the will of God revealed in his word, to the glory of God, deriving the principle of that life from Christ and the fresh supplies of grace from him -- and those who merely desire so to live, in whom God has wrought the willing, and who are troubled when it is otherwise.

Use the appeal to the writer's life as a test the hearer can apply. He had seen the doctrine, the conduct founded on it, the object in view, the fidelity, the long-suffering toward those who opposed and tried to lessen that authority, and the patience under adversity; he was therefore capable of judging between his teacher and the false ones, whose doctrine, conduct, motives and temper he could set beside them. Then state the rule without exception and tell the hearers to count the cost: so opposite is the whole of Christianity to the spirit and practice of the world that whoever gives himself entirely to God will be reviled and persecuted; and if religion gives no quarter to vice, the vicious will give none to religion. Those who think themselves religious and are not persecuted in some shape on that account deceive themselves. Add the saddest note in the chapter -- that a man who has begun to deceive others is the less likely to recover from his own error.

Set the example before the hearer as the writer sets it before his disciple, and draw the rule out of it: the more fully we know the doctrine of Christ and the apostles, the more closely we shall cleave to it, and the reason many sit loose to it is that they do not fully know it. Observe what follows from that -- the apostles had no enemies but those who did not know them, or did not know them fully, and those who knew them best loved and honoured them most. Note too what made such knowledge possible, that nothing was kept back but the whole counsel of God declared, so that if the hearers failed to know it the fault was their own; and say what an advantage it was to be trained up under such a teacher.

debates.question: Why are Antioch, Iconium and Lystra singled out?

sides.position: For the general reader they were good examples of what had often happened since; but for this reader they were the cities of the first journey, some incidents among his earliest experiences of the work
Because they were done in the country where Timothy lived, so he knew their truth not only from the writer's mouth but from others, and perhaps witnessed some himself
They are the three cities of the narrative in Acts, to which the party afterwards returned though they had so lately been persecuted there

outliers.note: Alone asks why these three cities were chosen out of a long history of suffering, and gives a double answer: for a general reader they were fair samples of what happened often afterwards, but for this reader they were the cities of the first missionary journey, some of the incidents among his earliest memories of the work and others just before he was taken as a companion.

Alone defines what persecution consists in -- subjecting a man to injury or disadvantage on account of his opinions, which is a different thing from meeting those opinions with argument -- and alone states the growth of bad men as a general law of an unconverted nature, so that Timothy was to expect no relief from any improvement in them.

Alone turns the rule into an instruction to count the cost and leaves no room for exceptions, holding that either the truth of scripture fails or those who think themselves religious and are not persecuted in some shape deceive themselves; and alone observes that a man who has begun to deceive others is the less likely to recover from his own error.

themes: But thou hast fully known my doctrine, manner of life, purpose, faith, longsuffering, charity, patience
Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution
But evil men and seducers shall wax worse and worse, deceiving, and being deceived

14.pericope_label: Continue thou; from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures

schools.summary: Mark the emphatic contrast at the head of the verse -- the others advance toward the worse, but thou abide -- and note that the verb for being assured is a rare one meaning to be made reliable. Then handle the textual question: the word rendered "of whom" may be singular or plural, the older authorities nearly balanced, and the choice decides whether the appeal is to the apostle alone or to a wider company. If you take the singular, say that the reminiscence of mother and grandmother is too slight to be introduced into so solemn an exhortation, and is covered by the next verse in any case. On the writings, note that the phrase used occurs nowhere else in the New Testament though Josephus has it, that the Old Testament is exclusively meant, and that the word for child denotes the unborn, the infant and the suckling alike, so that an early age is asserted without a precise one.

Take the exhortation as one suitable to every age and treat what follows as the reasons enforcing it. Then supply the background that makes the second reason weigh: the Jews taught their children the scriptures very early, the Alexandrian saying from their very infancy, and it was a maxim that a child of five was old enough to be taught them; the mother being a Jewess would have trained him so. Say that this highly becomes Christian parents and is part of the nurture and admonition of the Lord in which children are to be brought up. On the man of God at the close, allow the wider sense -- anyone in special relation to God, chosen by the Father, redeemed by the Son, called by the Spirit -- while noting that the title passed over from the prophets and applies especially to a minister.

Guard against presumption at the outset: no man, however well instructed in the things of God or grounded in divine grace, is beyond the reach of temptation, apostasy and final ruin, which is why watching unto prayer and continuing in the faith are necessary to the end. Then use the second argument as the sources use it. Christianity is founded on the law and the prophets, so a hearer who knew those writings from childhood could compare the new doctrine with all that had been typified and predicted and be assured it was true. But state the limit plainly: no soul is made wise unto salvation by those scriptures except as it refers everything to Christ, and the Jews who know them well remain unsaved because they do not believe in him. Then argue from the lesser to the greater -- only the older writings were extant in that childhood, and how much more are both Testaments together able to make us wise.

Keep this practical, because the passage is about a habit and not a theory. Those who would learn the things of God and be assured of them must know the holy scriptures, for they are the divine revelation, and the age of children is the age to learn. Say what the failure looks like: the books lying by us neglected, seldom or never looked into. Say what they are for: profitable for all purposes of the Christian life, of use to all, since all need to be taught, corrected and reproved, and there is something in them suitable for every case. Then close on the two applications that follow -- that we best oppose error by promoting a solid knowledge of the word of truth, and that the greatest kindness we can do children is to make them early know the Bible.

debates.question: From whom had Timothy learned these things?

sides.position: From the apostle: the singular reading is supported by the Syriac and Latin versions, and the reminiscence of mother and grandmother is too slight for so solemn an exhortation and is covered by the next verse
From a teacher approved of God

From his mother as well as the apostle; and having received truth from a parent's lips is a strong reason for holding to it, since a parent has no motive to deceive and has had better opportunity of examining what is true
From a list including the Old Testament prophets, the apostle, Eunice and Lois; there ought to be moral authority in such personages

outliers.note: Alone rejects the reading that finds the mother and grandmother in this clause, holding such a reminiscence, however touching, too slight to be introduced into so solemn an exhortation and covered in any case by the verse immediately following; and alone draws from the imperative a principle about the content rather than the man, that however the opposition intensifies there is to be no development in the fundamental doctrines.

Alone builds a doctrine on the parental reading he adopts, that having received the truth from a parent's lips is a strong reason for holding to it, since a parent has no motive to deceive a child and has usually had far better opportunity of examining what is true; and alone adds the qualification that this is not the highest motive and does not bind a man to what he afterwards finds erroneous.

Alone contrasts the sacred writings with the famous Ephesian writings that were profane rather than holy, and alone dates the teaching from the fifth year before breaking off to wish that Christian parents took like pains now.

themes: But continue thou in the things which thou hast learned and hast been assured of, knowing of whom thou hast learned them
And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus

16.pericope_label: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable

schools.summary: This verse turns on where the copula belongs, since the Greek supplies none, so lay the problem out honestly before choosing. The article is absent, and there are examples of that construction going both ways, so the words may be rendered all scripture or every scripture; and the verb may be inserted before the conjunction or after it, giving either a flat assertion that all scripture is inspired and profitable, or a statement that every inspired scripture is also profitable. If you prefer the second, argue it from the versions and from sense: a declaration of the inspiration of the Jewish scriptures would have been uncalled for here, since a trained Jew of that century would never have dreamt of doubting it and nothing in the preceding verses provokes it. Note that the compound adjective is a late word occurring only here, perhaps set against the commandments of men elsewhere. On the closing adjectives, the first comes from a root meaning to fit and the second is a rare verb for furnishing out completely; take the man of God as the Christian generally and not as an official title.

Take the words of the whole of holy scripture, the New Testament as well as the Old -- most of it was written by then, and the principle holds of what remained to be written, since all alike is breathed by God. Then commend the writings from their own marks, which is the argument this school can make and the grammarians cannot: the majesty and loftiness of the style, in many places inimitable by men, and the sublimity of the matter, transcending all human capacity ever to have attained or discovered -- the trinity of persons in the Godhead, the incarnation, the resurrection of the dead. On the man of God, allow the wider sense but note that the title passed over from the prophets and belongs especially to a minister of the gospel; and say what the design of the writings is, that preacher and hearer alike might have a perfect knowledge of the will of God, nothing wanting for the information of either.

Take the rendering that makes inspiration the qualifier -- every writing divinely inspired is profitable -- noting that the conjunction is dropped by almost all the versions and many of the fathers. Restrict the reference to the older writings, since the New Testament was neither collected nor complete when this was written. Then name the two accounts men have given of how inspiration worked, that every thought and word was dictated, or that God gave the matter and left the writers their own language, which would explain the variety of style. Add the claim that belongs to this school and to no other here: the Spirit who once inspired those who wrote also continually inspires and supernaturally assists those who read with earnest prayer. On the minister, be exacting -- he should be a man of the soundest sense and most cultivated mind, who has prayed much, read much and studied much, and takes up the work as from God.

Ask why the appeal to the scriptures comes just here, and answer from what follows rather than from what precedes. The writer has a great and sad thing to say next about his own death, so he offers much consolation first, and this from the most perfect source. Measure the disciple's grief by a case the hearers know: if the prophet who stayed with his master to the last breath rent his garments when he saw him taken, what must this disciple suffer, so loving and so beloved, on hearing that his master was about to die and that he could not even be near him -- for we are less grateful for the past time when we have been deprived of more recent company. Then show how the death is spoken of, in words meant to fill him with joy rather than grief: as a sacrifice and not a death, a migration and a removal to a better state.

debates.question: How should the opening clause be rendered?

sides.position: "Every scripture inspired by God is also profitable," on the authority of the older versions and a line of expositors, and because a declaration of the inspiration of the Jewish scriptures would have been uncalled for here
"Every writing divinely inspired is profitable"; the conjunction is omitted by almost all the versions and many of the fathers and does not agree well with the text
The received reading: this is the solemn testimony of the apostle that the whole of the older canon is inspired
The grammar will not settle it. The article is absent, there are examples both ways, and with no copula in the Greek one may insert the verb before the conjunction or after it
To the Old Testament only, since the New was neither collected nor complete when this was written
To the Old Testament, though the preferred rendering does not exclude the recent sacred compositions whose divine origin the writer knew
Properly to the Old Testament, and it includes the whole of it
To the whole of holy scripture, the New as well as the Old, most of which was now written; and it holds also of what was still to be written

debates.question: Who is the man of God?

sides.position: No official designation at all, but simply the Christian generally, striving to live a life pleasing to God
The preacher of righteousness, the minister who derives his commission from God and appears as his herald and servant
Anyone in special relation to God, but more especially a minister, the title having passed over from the prophets
He that is united to and approved of God

outliers.note: Alone declines to decide the construction, setting out both possibilities -- the absent article, the examples running both ways, and the missing copula which may be inserted before the conjunction or after it -- and concluding that so far as grammatical usage goes either rendering is open.

Alone extends the words to the New Testament as well as the Old, and to what remained to be written; and alone commends the writings from internal marks, the majesty and loftiness of a style in many places inimitable by men and the sublimity of matter transcending all human capacity ever to have discovered.

Alone traces the compound adjective through its parallels, the breath into the nostrils of Adam, the breathing on the disciples, a Greek moralist's usage and a Roman's phrase about a poet filled as by some divine spirit, and then alone insists on the limit, that the word asserts a fact and tells us nothing whatever about the manner of inspiration.
Alone claims that the Spirit who once inspired the writers continually inspires and supernaturally assists those who read the writings with earnest prayer.

Alone explains why the appeal to scripture stands just here, that the writer has a great and sad thing to say next about his own death and offers consolation first; he measures the disciple's grief by the prophet who rent his garments when his master was taken, and notes that the death is spoken of as a sacrifice and a migration rather than a death.

themes: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness
That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works
